title: The Tragedy of the Commons
subject: econ
paras: In 1968, the ecologist Garrett Hardin published an influential essay titled "The Tragedy of the Commons." Hardin asked readers to imagine a pasture open to all the herders in a village. Each herder gains the full benefit of adding one more animal to the pasture, while the cost of overgrazing is shared by everyone. As a result, each herder has a reason to keep adding animals, even though the combined effect is to destroy the pasture on which all of them depend.

Economists describe such a pasture as a common-pool resource. Two features define it. First, it is difficult to prevent people from using it. Second, one person's use reduces what is left for others. Ocean fisheries, groundwater, and forests often share these features, and many of them have suffered from overuse. The collapse of the Atlantic cod fishery off Newfoundland in the early 1990s, after decades of heavy fishing, is a frequently cited example.

Hardin concluded that there were only two solutions: dividing the commons into private property, so that each owner bears the costs of overuse, or placing it under government control. Both approaches have been tried. Governments set fishing quotas and limit the number of permits, and some countries have given fishers transferable shares of the total catch.

However, the political scientist Elinor Ostrom challenged the idea that these were the only options. Studying cases around the world, from mountain pastures in Switzerland to irrigation systems in Nepal and fisheries in Turkey, she found that many communities had managed shared resources successfully for centuries without either privatization or central control. These communities created their own rules about who could use the resource and how much, monitored one another, and applied gradually increasing penalties to those who broke the rules.

Ostrom identified conditions that made such self-governance more likely to succeed, including clear boundaries, rules suited to local circumstances, and ways for users to take part in making the rules. Her work earned her the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2009, making her the first woman to receive it. Today, most researchers see the tragedy of the commons not as an inevitable outcome but as a risk that depends on how a resource is governed.

opts: The village requires it.
Each herder gets the full benefit while the cost is shared.
The pasture grows larger each year.
Animals are cheap to buy.

is hard to keep people from using and is reduced by each use
can never be used up
is controlled by the government

To show that fishing quotas always work
To describe Hardin's childhood
To argue that cod are not valuable

a herder

She agreed that only governments can manage resources.

monitoring of users
increasing penalties for rule breakers

qs.q: Select THREE answer choices that express the most important ideas of the passage. Introductory sentence: Hardin's "tragedy of the commons" describes how shared resources can be overused.
opts: When individuals benefit fully from using a shared resource but share the costs, overuse can result.
Hardin argued that only privatization or government control could prevent the tragedy.
Ostrom showed that many communities successfully govern shared resources through their own rules.
Ostrom studied irrigation systems in Nepal.
The cod fishery collapsed in the early 1990s.
Hardin was an ecologist, not an economist.
